parameters.content:
## Check consent before embedding records into a pgvector index

Hundreds of workflows load documents, chunk them and push them into a vector store. Almost none ask
whether they are allowed to. This one puts a gate in front of the index: every record is checked
against a consent register first, and anything without a lawful basis is refused with its reason.

### How it works
Records waiting to be indexed and the consent register are read separately, because in real setups
the two live in different systems.

Each record then gets one decision with six independent refusal grounds. Special category data is
refused outright, because it needs its own Article 9 condition rather than ordinary consent.
Withdrawn consent stops anything new being indexed. An objection to profiling refuses the record
even when consent exists. Retention that has run out refuses it even though the consent was once
valid. And purpose limitation is the one most pipelines get wrong: consent for support or marketing
is not consent to be embedded into a model index.

A record whose register entry is missing the fields the decision needs is **held**, not refused.
Undecidable is a third answer, and guessing either way is what this exists to prevent.

Eligible records are embedded. Every decision and its ground goes into an inclusion manifest, so
months later you can prove exactly what was in the index and why.

### Setup
1. Create the consent register, documents and manifest tables, and enable the pgvector extension.
2. Connect Postgres, an embeddings provider and Slack.
3. Open **Consent Rules** and set `required_purpose` to the exact purpose string your register uses.

A refusal here is a legal decision, so the ground is recorded, never just a count.

## 1. Read the records and the register separately
The queue and the register usually live in different systems, so they are read
apart and joined here rather than in one SQL statement.

## 2. One decision, six grounds, three answers
Eligible, refused with the exact ground, or held because the register cannot
answer. Held is not a soft refusal. It is a third answer.

## 3. Only eligible records reach the index
Everything else stops at the branch on the left. Long text is split before it
is embedded, so a record does not silently lose its tail.

## 4. Record what went in
The manifest is written per record, so the index can be proved later rather
than described.

## 5. Refused and held records stop here
Both are stored with the ground that produced them. Held rows are the ones a
human still has to answer.

## 6. One run, one message
Four branches merge before counting, so a run reports once. Refusals are
grouped by ground, because a bare count tells nobody what to fix.
